prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical discovery of the Z2 topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall state, and for its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B008 as a single part to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. After the full exchange I still think it is the one candidate on the shortlist where the discovery is a new state of matter, a bulk insulator whose helical edge states are protected by time-reversal symmetry and spin-orbit coupling and classified by a Z2 invariant, not by a broken symmetry. The chronology is the cleanest the committee can ask for: a minimal-model prediction (Kane and Mele, 2005), a concrete material proposal, and a quantized-edge-conductance experiment in HgTe/CdTe wells (Molenkamp's group, 2007). Independent confirmation by transport, ARPES, STM and first-principles band-structure calculations makes the claim checkable and not a matter of trust. The concept has since spread to photonics, cold atoms, phononics and materials design. It also has the broadest opening support on the shortlist (six of eight top-three placements, and the same trio proposed by everyone who proposed laureates). Round 1 sharpened my view that the citation must name the Z2 state and its first observation, not topological matter in general, and that wording answers the chair's question about adjacency to the 2016 prize.
statement.case_against: The attribution objection is real and was raised by six colleagues. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe system that told Molenkamp where to look, and the 3D generalization (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Roy; Hasan's ARPES) lies outside the three names. Zhang's death in 2018 removes a claimant but not the question. I accept that I had under-weighted how decisive the BHZ proposal was for the experiment; I still think the conceptual origin is the Z2 insight of Kane and Mele, but a reasonable member can hold the opposite view and I cannot prove otherwise from the literature alone. The 2016 prize is a further point against, though I think it covered a different discovery. Applications remain limited, and edge-transport protection in real devices is subtler than the clean picture. Finally, B035 is the stronger configuration on credit and has far more explicit first-choice support, so I could be wrong that the conceptual novelty of B008 outweighs its messier attribution.

responses.point: Pearce (chair) argues that crediting the measured result to Molenkamp while omitting the proposal he tested is the kind of attribution the committee should avoid, and that lattice clocks have a cleaner chain from proposal to demonstration to precision frontier.
responses.response: This is the most serious objection and I have changed my mind about its weight, though not my vote. I conceded in round 1 that BHZ is a weakness; I now accept it is more than a footnote, because BHZ named the system and the parameter regime (the critical HgTe well thickness) that made the experiment possible. My answer is the wording. The citation is built on the Z2 quantum spin Hall state and its first observation, and it does not claim to settle everything in topological matter. Kane and Mele supplied the state and the invariant; Molenkamp's group made the sample and measured the quantized edge conductance, which is an experimental achievement in its own right. Where I differ from you is that a three-name ceiling always leaves someone out of a theory-and-experiment story, and the question should be whether the omission distorts the discovery. For the Z2 state I do not think it does. I still agree B035 has the cleaner chain and I regard it as the main competitor.

responses.point: Johansson says the BHZ problem is not minor, since BHZ made the prediction that told Molenkamp where to look, and that the 2016 topological prize is a closer precedent than I acknowledged.
responses.response: On BHZ I now agree with you that I was too brisk; I have said above that it narrows the case. On 2016 I still disagree, and I would ask the committee to apply the same test to B008 and B035. The 2016 prize honoured topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall and Haldane lineage, whose invariant is the Chern number and needs no time-reversal symmetry or spin-orbit coupling. The Z2 state is protected by time-reversal symmetry and has no Hall conductance, so it is a different class and was confirmed by a different experiment. That is the same kind of distinction the lattice-clock supporters draw between a clock on a lattice and the comb or ion clocks of 2005 and 2012. If adjacency disqualifies B008 it should weigh equally on B035; I would rather the committee judge each by whether the new concept is distinct, and I think both pass narrowly.

responses.point: Kroll asks condensed-matter members to say how decisive the BHZ proposal was, and says he would support B008 if the topological case can be settled with a trio that credits the theory fairly.
responses.response: Since you asked directly: the BHZ proposal was decisive for choosing HgTe and for the thickness at which the inverted band structure appears, and Molenkamp's group would probably have found the effect later without it, but the state itself and its Z2 classification come from Kane and Mele. I would say BHZ was decisive for the experiment, not for the discovery. That is a judgment, not a fact the committee can read off, and I would support asking an expert report to check the chronology, which I only have from memory. I accept your point that the lattice clock has no such problem. I also noted your remark about a possible B035 plus B008 pairing; with a three-person ceiling I do not think two parts can be made to work (two plus three names is five), so I am no longer pursuing it.

responses.point: Lindroth agrees B008 is the strongest conceptual discovery on the list but disagrees with my ranking of lattice clocks sixth, arguing that a measurement prize does not need to be justified by overlap alone.
responses.response: I accept that criticism. My sixth place came from caution about the 2005 and 2012 prizes and from my own distance from atomic physics, not from doubt about the clock results, and your point about atomic-structure theory (magic wavelengths, blackbody shifts) checked against independent clocks is the sort of calculation-plus-measurement agreement I value. After round 1 I regard B035 as a legitimate first-rank candidate and I keep it as my first alternative. What still separates us is what a citation should reward. You and I both apply a standard of surprise about nature, and I think the Z2 state meets it more clearly than a gain in precision, even though I concede that the lattice clock is a new capability. I do not think it is cleaner on credit and I will say so in the vote.

uncertainties: How the committee should weigh the BHZ proposal against the Kane-Mele Z2 insight; I think the discovery is credited correctly but that is a contestable judgment.
Whether an expert report would confirm my memory of the chronology (Kane-Mele 2005, BHZ 2006, Molenkamp 2007) and the credit for choosing HgTe.
Whether the committee will accept that the 2016 prize covers a different class of state, or applies one adjacency standard to both B008 and B035.

I defer to colleagues on the weight of B035 and B023, which are outside my field, and the five-member first-choice support for B035 is a signal I take seriously without treating it as a substitute for the scientific case.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B008: my work is computational magnetism and electronic structure, not topological insulators, and I have no personal or institutional tie to Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. For B051 or B020 there is only intellectual overlap with correlated-electron physics, not a recusal issue. I note the disclosures by Johansson, Olsson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce; none concerns B008 or my alternatives, and I do not ask anyone to step back.
